markdown:
**In brief**

- The Conservative front bench pressed the Government on whether the Courts and Tribunals Bill would reduce jury access, as when Nick Timothy asked whether the Justice Secretary could "guarantee that the Bill will not reduce access to jury trials at all?" [Source 1]
- The Justice Secretary tied his approach to court backlogs, as when Alex Norris said "my priority is to reduce the Crown court waiting list and enable victims to have their day in court more quickly." [Source 5]
- The Liberal Democrat spokesperson raised human rights and scrutiny time, as when Jessica Brown-Fuller said "The time is right to change course, prior to the return of the Bill in October." [Source 9]

**Conservative frontbench - critical**

Conservative spokespeople challenged the Government over its jury proposals, as when Nick Timothy, Shadow Justice Secretary, quoted the Prime Minister's promise to "find ways of not reducing access to jury trial." [Source 1]

- Timothy also cited the Prime Minister's description of jury trials as a "linchpin of a fair society." [Source 1]
- Neil Shastri-Hurst, a shadow health minister, who spoke on a justice question, referred to reports of a possible amendment under which a judge would decide on jury or single-judge trial in either-way offences. He said the legal profession had warned this "will lead to satellite litigation, with repeated appeals, and slow down the legal process." [Source 6] He asked: "Will the Government finally listen to the legal profession, or will they plough on regardless?" [Source 6]

**Government - focused on reducing delays**

The Lord Chancellor, Alex Norris, framed the Bill around delays, as when he said "I have been clear that my priority is to reduce the Crown court waiting list and enable victims to have their day in court more quickly." [Source 5]

- He told the House that the Bill will return on 13 October [Source 5].
- Responding to a request to engage, he said "if people have an interest in the legislation and want to discuss it, our door is open." [Source 8]

**Liberal Democrats - critical, citing rights and scrutiny**

Jessica Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson, argued the Bill should change course, as when she cited Amnesty International's description of the proposals as a "dilution of the quality of justice" [Source 9].

- She said "the Government batted away our concerns" [Source 9] at earlier stages.
- She asked for a guarantee that Members and experts would have "adequate time to scrutinise the Government's amendments" [Source 9] before debate on the second day back after recess.

About the evidence: The records cover one Commons Justice question session on 15 September 2026, with contributions from two Conservative frontbenchers, one Liberal Democrat and the Lord Chancellor. No backbench speeches or division records are included. Two further results, from 2012, concern Northern Ireland, not trial by jury, so they are not used.
